measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a policy to the county charter’s preamble making long-term resilience to extreme weather a county priority, including fire, flooding, wind, rain, heat, drought and sea-level rise. The policy calls for collaboration with cities, districts and other public entities.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve this addition to the county charter.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed charter addition.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a statement to the county charter’s preamble affirming the dignity, civil rights and equal protection of county residents, and a commitment to equity, fairness, inclusion, belonging, accessibility and opportunity.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve this addition to the county charter.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed charter addition.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Gives the Board of Supervisors 60 days, instead of 30, to appoint someone or call a special election when an elected county office other than a Board seat becomes vacant. Before appointing someone, the Board must hold at least one publicly noticed meeting for comments on the appointment and candidates’ qualifications. If the Board does not act within 60 days, the elections officer must call a special election.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the 60-day deadline and public-meeting requirement.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these changes and retain the current 30-day deadline.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Requires an independent redistricting commission, governed by state law, to redraw the county’s five supervisorial districts after each federal census. The Board of Supervisors currently adopts those boundaries by ordinance. Supervisors would still be elected by district, live in the district represented and serve four-year terms, limited to three consecutive terms.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve independent-commission redistricting after each federal census.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this change and retain the Board’s current redistricting process.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a sales tax for 14 years: 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties, and 1% in San Francisco. The district estimates about $980 million a year. After specified costs, money would fund public transit, reduced fares and transfers, accessibility and other listed programs under the measure’s county allocation formulas. Repaving roads served by fixed-route transit is allowed in the four counties outside San Francisco. The measure requires independent oversight and specified financial reviews; transit funding may be withheld for noncompliance. Approval requires a majority across the entire five-county district.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the proposed sales tax for 14 years throughout the five-county district.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed regional sales tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allows Burlingame Elementary School District to borrow up to $100 million for listed school repairs, classroom and lab improvements, technology, safety and accessibility projects. Property taxes would repay the bonds. The district estimates an average annual tax of $16 per $100,000 of assessed value and about $195.5 million in total principal and interest, with repayment anticipated through fiscal year 2057–58. Actual taxes and repayment depend on bond sales and assessed values. It requires independent oversight and annual financial and performance audits. Regular salaries and operating expenses are excluded, except staff costs for work on bond projects. Approval requires 55% of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize up to $100 million in school bonds, repaid through property taxes under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this authorization to issue the proposed bonds.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replaces Cabrillo Unified School District’s current parcel tax with a $239 annual tax per taxable parcel from July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2032, estimated to raise $2.6 million a year. Money is restricted to listed teaching, staffing, career and college preparation, student support, special education, transportation and arts programs; administrator salaries, benefits and pensions are excluded. Owner-occupants may apply for an exemption if they are 65 before May 1 of the tax year, receive Supplemental Security Income for disability, or receive Social Security Disability Insurance with income at or below 250% of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines. The application is due by May 1; existing qualifying exemptions continue. It requires public reporting and independent oversight. Approval requires two-thirds of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the replacement $239 annual parcel tax for five years, with the stated exemptions and restrictions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed replacement parcel tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replaces Jefferson Union High School District’s $58 parcel tax with a $98 annual tax per taxable parcel for ten years beginning in fiscal year 2027–28, estimated to raise $3.4 million a year. Money would support teachers, academic programs, career training, college preparation and school staff; administrator salaries, benefits and pensions are excluded. Owner-occupants age 65 or older may apply for an exemption, and existing senior exemptions continue. It requires annual reporting and citizens’ oversight. If the tax causes a reduction in state or federal funding, the tax must be reduced as needed to restore that funding. Approval requires two-thirds of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the replacement $98 annual parcel tax for ten years under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed replacement parcel tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Renews Pacifica School District’s parcel tax for July 1, 2027 through June 30, 2037, starting at $118 per taxable parcel each year and adjusting annually for regional inflation. The district estimates $1.3 million a year for listed academic, arts, library, technology and student-support programs and teachers. Exemptions are available to owner-occupants age 65 or older as of July 1, disability recipients of Supplemental Security Income, and Social Security Disability Insurance recipients with income no higher than 250% of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines, under the application rules. Administrator salaries and benefits are excluded. Annual public reports and the citizens’ oversight committee would track spending. Approval requires two-thirds of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the ten-year parcel-tax renewal with annual inflation adjustments and the stated exemptions and restrictions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed renewal of the expiring parcel tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replaces San Carlos School District’s existing parcel tax with an annual $489 tax per taxable parcel, adjusted each year by the Bay Area Consumer Price Index, for up to eight years beginning July 1, 2027. The district estimates $4.4 million a year for teachers, class sizes, academic programs, libraries and arts; administrator salaries and pensions are excluded. Owner-occupants may apply for exemptions if they are 65 or older as of July 1, receive Supplemental Security Income for disability, or receive Social Security Disability Insurance with income no higher than 250% of the 2012 federal poverty guidelines. Existing qualifying exemptions continue. It requires annual reporting and independent citizens’ oversight. Approval requires two-thirds of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve this replacement parcel tax, starting at $489 a year with annual inflation adjustments, for up to eight years.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed replacement parcel tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allows San Mateo County Community College District to borrow up to $848 million for listed classroom, career-training, infrastructure, technology, safety and other college-facility projects. Property taxes would repay the bonds. The district estimates an average annual tax of $10.50 and a highest annual tax of $18 per $100,000 of assessed value and about $1.35 billion in total principal and interest, with repayment anticipated through fiscal year 2048–49. Actual taxes and repayment depend on bond sales and assessed values. It requires citizens’ oversight and annual financial and performance audits. Regular salaries and operating expenses are excluded, except staff costs for work on bond projects. Approval requires 55% of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize up to $848 million in college-district bonds, repaid through property taxes under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this authorization to issue the proposed bonds.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allows San Mateo-Foster City School District to borrow up to $498 million for listed classroom, skilled-trades and science projects, building repairs, safety, accessibility, facilities and affordable teacher/staff housing. Property taxes would repay the bonds. The district estimates an average annual tax of $29 per $100,000 of assessed value and about $900 million in total principal and interest, with repayment anticipated through fiscal year 2054–55. Actual taxes and repayment depend on bond sales and assessed values. It requires citizens’ oversight and annual financial and performance audits. Regular salaries and operating expenses are excluded, except staff costs for work on bond projects. Approval requires 55% of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize up to $498 million in school bonds, repaid through property taxes under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this authorization to issue the proposed bonds.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Creates an annual tax beginning July 1, 2027 to build, operate, staff, maintain and improve a community center and its programs. Initial rates are 33 cents per square foot of dwelling-unit improvements and 54 cents per square foot for other improvements, with about $7.1 million estimated in the first year. The Council may later raise rates within the measure’s limits based on the greater of regional inflation or statewide per-person income growth. Owner-occupants age 65 or older by June 30 before the applicable tax year and legally tax-exempt property are exempt under the application rules. Money goes into a restricted community-center fund with annual audits. The measure also increases the city’s spending limit for four years. The tax continues until voters end it; a majority vote is required.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the proposed community-center tax and spending-limit increase under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed community-center tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Replaces most Brisbane business-license tax formulas with $50 for businesses with annual gross receipts of $25,000 or less, and $50 plus $1 per $1,000 of receipts above $25,000 for most other businesses. For this calculation, the tax base cannot be below operating costs. It removes exemptions for charitable/nonprofit organizations, newspapers, café musicians, real-estate auctioneers, veterans and residential rentals with fewer than five units. Separate taxes for cannabis, hotels, liquid storage, capital improvements/residential construction, outdoor advertising and recycling remain. The city estimates $1 million in additional annual general-purpose revenue. The tax continues until voters repeal it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve this revised business-license tax structure.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these changes and retain the current tax structure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Raises Burlingame’s tax on hotel and other temporary lodging stays of less than 30 continuous days from 12% to 15%. The guest pays the tax. The city estimates an additional $5.7 million a year for general city purposes, with annual public audits. The rate continues until voters amend or repeal it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the increase from 12% to 15%.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the increase and retain the current 12% rate.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Allows East Palo Alto to borrow up to $125 million for a library and civic center, police/emergency facilities, water and stormwater infrastructure, and land for recreation and parks. Property taxes would repay the bonds, whose interest rate could not exceed 12%. The city estimates an average annual tax of $105.26 per $100,000 of assessed value, a highest rate of $114.41 beginning in fiscal year 2028–29, final collection in 2057–58, and total principal and interest of $268,205,658. These are estimates. Funds are restricted to the listed improvements, with annual independent financial audits and public reports. Approval requires two-thirds of votes cast.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize up to $125 million in city bonds, repaid through property taxes under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this authorization to issue the proposed bonds.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Limits East Palo Alto City Council service to three consecutive four-year terms. A partial term longer than two years counts as a full term. Only terms beginning after the ordinance takes effect count toward the limit; earlier service does not count.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt these prospective City Council term limits.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these term limits and retain the current rules without a term limit.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Changes the map used to define Half Moon Bay’s Downtown Area under its residential-growth rules, replacing the 1998 redevelopment-survey area with the Local Coastal Land Use Plan’s Town Center Map. Among affected residential parcels, 286 would be added to Downtown and 40 removed; 491 parcels of all types are affected. The measure makes corresponding coastal-plan and municipal-code changes. California Coastal Commission certification is required before the changes take effect.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the proposed Downtown boundary changes, subject to Coastal Commission certification.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these changes and retain the current Downtown definition.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Approves four agreements with Mercy Housing for a 40-unit affordable housing development for senior agricultural workers and 2,653 square feet of community space on city-owned land at 535–555 Kelly Avenue. They include a 99-year ground lease at $1 a year, development and financing conditions, affordability and preference requirements, and recorded notices and restrictions. The City Manager could execute and implement the agreements and must review the ground lease at least every seven years. The ordinance also makes the stated environmental-exemption findings.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve Ordinance 2026-01 and the proposed housing agreements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject adoption of Ordinance 2026-01 and these proposed agreements.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Requires a separate majority vote before the city sells, leases, conveys, declares surplus, changes the use of, or permanently alters any of eight city-owned downtown parking plazas in a way that reduces parking availability, access or convenience. This includes housing projects that reduce parking. Maintenance and improvements intended to preserve or improve parking, and temporary community events lasting no more than three consecutive days, are exempt. Covered actions taken since May 15, 2025 would be void unless reenacted and voter-approved. Future amendments or repeal also require a public vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve these voter-approval requirements for the downtown parking plazas.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these requirements and retain the current decision process.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a 1% city sales tax, or $1 per $100 of taxable purchases, estimated to raise $5 million a year for any general city purpose. State-law exemptions, including groceries and prescription medicines, remain. Spending requires annual public audits. The tax continues until voters end it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% city sales tax.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed additional sales tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Makes Portola Valley a charter town with the specified local-tax powers and authorizes a real-property transfer tax of $10 per $1,000 of consideration paid. The current rate is 27.5 cents per $500. The tax applies to transfers for payment, with listed exemptions; buyers and sellers are jointly liable but may negotiate who pays. The Council may reduce or eliminate the rate and add exemptions, but voters must approve an increase above the authorized rate. The town estimates $2 million in additional annual general-purpose revenue. It requires annual independent audits and Finance and Audit Committee review. The authorization continues until voters end it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the proposed charter and real-property transfer tax.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the proposed charter and transfer-tax changes.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adopts rent and eviction rules. Covered multifamily units built before February 1, 1995 would use October 29, 2025 rents, or initial rents for later tenancies, as the base. Annual increases would be 60% of local inflation, with a 0% floor and 5% ceiling; unused increases cannot carry forward, and adjustment petitions are available. Just-cause eviction rules expand to more housing, including single-family homes, ADUs, affordable housing and mobile homes, with additional notice and specified protections for older or disabled tenants and children or educators during the school year. For no-fault evictions, relocation assistance is the greater of four times monthly HUD fair-market rent or $12,000 per household, plus $6,000 for qualifying households with a tenant age 62 or older, disabled or terminally ill. The minimum and additional relocation payments adjust annually for inflation, and tenants must notify the landlord of eligibility for the additional payment. Tenants gain a right to return if the unit reenters the rental market. The measure also regulates repairs, buyouts, utility billing and enforcement. City administration is estimated at $5–11 million a year, paid through annual landlord fees. Initial fees are $120 per rent-controlled unit and $84 for other partially covered units until the Council sets fees sufficient to fund administration.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the proposed rent-control, eviction, relocation and administration rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these changes and retain the current rules.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Repeals the rule requiring a citywide vote before approving specified buildings over 50 feet or three stories, residential density above the 1974 limits, multistory parking, and changes affecting Crystal Springs Road between Oak Avenue and Junipero Serra Freeway, and Sneath Lane from El Camino Real to the western city limits. Covered projects would instead use the approval processes required by applicable city and state law, including zoning and environmental review.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Repeal these separate voter-approval requirements.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the existing voter-approval requirements.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Prohibits the sale, use and discharge of state-approved “safe and sane” fireworks in San Bruno by repealing the ordinance that currently allows their limited sale and use.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the prohibition on safe and sane fireworks.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the prohibition and retain the current limited sales and use rules.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Revises the annual business-license tax. Most businesses would pay $75 on the first $75,000 of gross receipts, plus a charge per $1,000 above that amount: $1 for general/retail businesses, $2 for professional/advanced services, $1.50 for property/rental activities, $1.50 for other services, and $2 for contractors. Existing separate taxes for cardrooms and airport parking remain. The city estimates $4 million a year for general city purposes. The tax continues until voters end it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the revised business-license tax rates and structure.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these changes and retain the current rates and structure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adds a 0.5% city sales tax, or 50 cents per $100 of taxable purchases, from April 1, 2027 through March 31, 2041 unless voters extend it. The city estimates $6 million a year for general city purposes. Existing exemptions, including groceries, prescription medicines and diapers, remain. Revenue requires independent audits and stays under local control.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional sales tax for 14 years.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed additional sales tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Raises the city’s own sales tax from 0.25% to 0.5%, an additional 25 cents per $100 of taxable purchases. The city estimates $7 million a year for general city purposes. State-law exemptions, including groceries and prescription medicines, remain. It requires annual audits and review by a five-member public committee. Collection starts on the first day of the calendar quarter beginning 110 days after election results are certified. The increase continues until voters end it.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 0.25% city sales tax.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this proposed increase.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Updates the charter to reflect the city’s existing district elections and census-based redistricting, and removes outdated election provisions. It extends the time to fill Council vacancies from 30 to 60 days, and the continuous absence that can cause loss of office without permission from 30 to 60 days. Council meeting schedules could be set by resolution. Emergency ordinances could be published in summary form and would no longer automatically expire on day 91. The measure also removes specified candidate-statement and newspaper-bidding requirements, clarifies the Finance Director’s title and appointment process, and adds gender-neutral wording.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve this package of charter amendments.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject these proposed charter amendments.

Section 67700 (Senate Bill 63/Connect Bay Area Act, Wiener/Arreguin, October l3, 2025)
created the Public Transit Revenue Measure District (“PTRMD” or “District”) with jurisdiction
extending throughout the territorial boundaries of the Counties ofAlameda, Contra Costa, San
Mateo, and Santa Clara, and the City and County of San Francisco, and provides that the District
shall be governed by the same board that governs the Metropolitan Transportation Commission
(“MTC”); and
